::: {.callout-note .objectives}
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- explain what a **dissimilarity matrix** is and what MDS tries to do with it;
- run **classical MDS** with `cmdscale()` and read its eigenvalues and goodness of fit;
- recognise **non-Euclidean** dissimilarities from **negative eigenvalues**;
- check a configuration with a **Shepard diagram**, and run **non-metric MDS** with `MASS::isoMDS()`;
- apply MDS to dissimilarities between objects that are not places (variables, mixed-type observations).
:::

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source(here::here("_common.R"))
```

```{r}
#| label: packages
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(MASS, include.only = c("isoMDS", "Shepard"))   # avoid masking dplyr::select
```

## 1. Why MDS?

Sometimes we do not have variables for our objects, only **how different they are from each other**: road distances between cities, how often people confuse two sounds, how dissimilar two products are judged to be, the genetic distance between species. Such a table is a **dissimilarity matrix**: a symmetric table with zeros on the diagonal, where entry $(i, j)$ says how far object $i$ is from object $j$.

**Multidimensional scaling (MDS)** answers: *can I place the objects as points on a plane (or in a few dimensions) so that the distances between points reproduce the dissimilarities?* If it works, the plot is a **map** of the objects, and we can look at it to find groups, gradients and outliers.

## 2. A table of road distances

`eurodist` contains the **road distances** (in km) between 21 European cities — not straight-line distances, and not all capitals (Calais, Cherbourg, Gibraltar, Hook of Holland, Lyons, Marseilles, Milan, Munich are included).

```{r}
#| label: eurodist
class(eurodist)
as.matrix(eurodist)[1:5, 1:5]
```

It is stored as a `dist` object: only the lower triangle is kept, because the table is symmetric.

## 3. Classical MDS with `cmdscale()`

```{r}
#| label: cmdscale
mds_euro <- cmdscale(eurodist, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
names(mds_euro)
head(round(mds_euro$points), 4)
```

`points` are the coordinates of the cities in a two-dimensional configuration. Classical MDS (also called *principal coordinates analysis*, PCoA) is closely related to PCA: it computes eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a matrix derived from the distances, and keeps the first `k` dimensions.

### Eigenvalues: some are negative!

```{r}
#| label: eigen
round(mds_euro$eig / 1e6, 2)          # in millions, for readability
sum(mds_euro$eig < 0)
```

If the distances were **Euclidean** (straight-line distances between points in some space), all eigenvalues would be $\ge 0$. Here `r sum(mds_euro$eig < 0)` eigenvalues are **negative**, the largest in absolute value being `r round(min(mds_euro$eig) / 1e6, 2)` million. Negative eigenvalues are the signature of **non-Euclidean** dissimilarities: no configuration of points, in any number of dimensions, reproduces road distances exactly. Roads bend around mountains and seas, and the Earth is not flat.

The negative eigenvalues are small compared with the first two (`r round(mds_euro$eig[1] / 1e6, 1)` and `r round(mds_euro$eig[2] / 1e6, 1)` million), so a 2-D map is still a good summary.

### Goodness of fit

`cmdscale()` returns two goodness-of-fit (GOF) measures for the `k` dimensions kept, with eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \dots$:

$$
\text{GOF}_1 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i}{\sum_{i} |\lambda_i|}, \qquad
\text{GOF}_2 = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{k} \lambda_i}{\sum_{i} \max(\lambda_i, 0)} .
$$

```{r}
#| label: gof
mds_euro$GOF
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## How to read the GOF

- **GOF₂** = `r round(mds_euro$GOF[2], 3)`: the two dimensions account for `r round(100 * mds_euro$GOF[2])`% of the sum of the **positive** eigenvalues.
- **GOF₁** = `r round(mds_euro$GOF[1], 3)` is smaller because its denominator also includes the **absolute values of the negative eigenvalues** — that is, it penalises the non-Euclidean part of the data.
- For Euclidean distances the two values coincide. A large gap between them is another sign that the dissimilarities are far from Euclidean.
:::

## 4. Turning the configuration into a map

```{r}
#| label: fig-raw
#| fig-cap: "Raw classical MDS configuration of the 21 cities, before any flipping."
cities <- data.frame(city = labels(eurodist),
                     dim1 = mds_euro$points[, 1],
                     dim2 = mds_euro$points[, 2])

ggplot(cities, aes(dim1, dim2, label = city)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.6, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Dimension 1 (km)", y = "Dimension 2 (km)")
```

Distances alone carry **no information about orientation**: rotating or mirroring the map does not change any distance. The signs of the MDS axes, like those of PCA components, are arbitrary. To make the map look like Europe we want west on the left and north at the top. Instead of guessing, we let the data decide using three cities we know:

```{r}
#| label: flip
if (cities$dim1[cities$city == "Lisbon"] > cities$dim1[cities$city == "Athens"]) {
  cities$dim1 <- -cities$dim1        # Lisbon must be west of Athens
}
if (cities$dim2[cities$city == "Stockholm"] < cities$dim2[cities$city == "Athens"]) {
  cities$dim2 <- -cities$dim2        # Stockholm must be north of Athens
}
```

With the configuration R returns here, axis 1 already had west on the left, while axis 2 had to be flipped (north was at the bottom). On another computer the signs may differ — which is exactly why we test instead of hard-coding a flip.

```{r}
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Classical MDS map of 21 European cities from road distances, oriented with west on the left and north at the top."
ggplot(cities, aes(dim1, dim2, label = city)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.6, size = 3) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "West – East (km)", y = "South – North (km)")
```

::: {.callout-tip .read-output}
## Reading the map

- The **Iberian** cities (Lisbon, Madrid, Gibraltar, and Barcelona further east) are on the far left.
- **Stockholm** and **Copenhagen** are at the top (north), with **Hamburg** below them.
- **Athens** is in the far south-east, and **Rome** south of **Milan**.
- The North Sea and Channel cities (**Calais**, **Brussels**, **Hook of Holland**, **Cherbourg**) and **Paris** form a cluster in the north-west centre; **Geneva**, **Lyons** and **Marseilles** lie between this cluster and the Mediterranean.

The geography is recognisable, but not perfect: the map is built from road distances, not coordinates.
:::

::: {.callout-note .deeper collapse="true"}
## Going deeper: double centring

Let $D^{(2)}$ be the matrix of **squared** dissimilarities and $J = I - \frac1n \mathbf 1 \mathbf 1^\top$ the centring matrix. Classical MDS computes

$$
B = -\tfrac12 \, J D^{(2)} J ,
$$

the **double-centred** matrix (rows and columns centred). If the dissimilarities are Euclidean distances between points $x_1, \dots, x_n$, then $B$ is exactly the matrix of inner products of the centred points, $B = XX^\top$, which is positive semi-definite. Writing $B = V \Lambda V^\top$, the coordinates are $X_k = V_k \Lambda_k^{1/2}$ — this is what `cmdscale()` returns. When the dissimilarities are not Euclidean, $B$ has negative eigenvalues and $\Lambda^{1/2}$ only exists for the positive ones.

```{r}
#| label: double-centre
D2 <- as.matrix(eurodist)^2
n  <- nrow(D2)
J  <- diag(n) - matrix(1 / n, n, n)
B  <- -0.5 * J %*% D2 %*% J
e  <- eigen(B, symmetric = TRUE)

X  <- e$vectors[, 1:2] %*% diag(sqrt(e$values[1:2]))
all.equal(abs(X), abs(unname(mds_euro$points)))   # same up to sign
```
:::

## 5. How good is the map? Shepard diagram

A **Shepard diagram** plots the original dissimilarities against the distances on the map. If the map were perfect, all points would lie on the diagonal.

```{r}
#| label: fig-shepard
#| fig-cap: "Shepard diagram: road distances versus distances on the 2-D MDS map. Each point is a pair of cities."
fitted_d <- dist(mds_euro$points)

shep <- data.frame(road = as.vector(eurodist),
                   map  = as.vector(fitted_d))

ggplot(shep, aes(road, map)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "#D55E00") +
  labs(x = "Road distance (km)", y = "Distance on the MDS map (km)")

cor(shep$road, shep$map)
```

The correlation between road and map distances is `r round(cor(shep$road, shep$map), 3)`. Most pairs are close to the diagonal. Which pairs are worst?

```{r}
#| label: worst-pairs
pairs <- t(combn(labels(eurodist), 2))   # same order as the dist object
shep |>
  mutate(from = pairs[, 1], to = pairs[, 2], error = map - road) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(error))) |>
  head(4)
```

Some entries cannot be reproduced by any flat map. For instance the table gives Athens–Rome as `r as.matrix(eurodist)["Athens", "Rome"]` km, which is *shorter* than the straight-line distance between the two cities (about 1,050 km). A few entries of this old table look inconsistent with geography, and MDS spreads their error over the whole map.

## 6. Non-metric MDS

Classical MDS tries to reproduce the dissimilarities **as numbers**. Often we only trust their **order**: "A is more similar to B than to C". Rating scales, rankings and many ecological dissimilarities are like this. **Non-metric MDS** looks for a configuration whose distances are in the **same rank order** as the dissimilarities, as far as possible.

The mismatch is measured by **Kruskal's stress** (0 = perfect). `MASS::isoMDS()` reports it **in percent**. Kruskal's rough guide: below 5% good, 5–10% fair, 10–20% poor, above 20% bad.

```{r}
#| label: isomds
iso_euro <- isoMDS(eurodist, k = 2, trace = FALSE)  # starts from cmdscale()
iso_euro$stress
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-iso-shepard
#| fig-cap: "Shepard diagram for non-metric MDS: the step line is the best monotone (order-preserving) fit."
sh <- Shepard(eurodist, iso_euro$points)
plot(sh, pch = 20, col = "grey50",
     xlab = "Road distance (km)", ylab = "Map distance")
lines(sh$x, sh$yf, type = "S", col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2)
```

The stress is `r round(iso_euro$stress, 1)`%. For road distances, metric and non-metric MDS give very similar maps; non-metric MDS really pays off when only the order of the dissimilarities is meaningful.

## 7. MDS beyond geography: a map of variables

MDS works with **any** dissimilarity. Let's draw a map of the 11 **variables** of `mtcars`, using a distance based on their correlation: strongly positively correlated variables should be close, negatively correlated ones far apart.

$$
d_{jk} = \sqrt{2(1 - r_{jk})}
$$

This is (up to a constant) the Euclidean distance between the standardised variables, so it ranges from 0 ($r = 1$) to 2 ($r = -1$).

```{r}
#| label: mtcars-mds
d_vars  <- as.dist(sqrt(2 * (1 - cor(mtcars))))
mds_var <- cmdscale(d_vars, k = 2, eig = TRUE)

round(mds_var$eig, 3)
mds_var$GOF
```

Because this distance *is* Euclidean, there are no (meaningfully) negative eigenvalues and the two GOF values coincide — a nice contrast with `eurodist`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-mtcars-mds
#| fig-cap: "MDS map of the variables of mtcars, from the distance sqrt(2(1 - r))."
data.frame(variable = rownames(mds_var$points), mds_var$points) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, label = variable)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.7) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "Dimension 1", y = "Dimension 2")
```

`mpg` lies on the opposite side of the map from `cyl`, `disp` and `wt` (strong negative correlations), and close to `drat` and `vs`. The second dimension separates `qsec` from `am`, `gear` and `carb`. This is the same structure that PCA of `mtcars` revealed in [the PCA lesson](50-pca.qmd) — but seen from the variables' side.

::: {.callout-warning .pitfall}
## Common pitfalls

1. **Assuming every distance table is Euclidean.** Road distances, Gower distances, rating-based dissimilarities usually are not; check the eigenvalues.
2. **Misreading `GOF`.** It is a pair of ratios of eigenvalue sums (with absolute or positive eigenvalues in the denominator), not squared values to be added.
3. **Interpreting the orientation or signs of MDS axes.** Distances are unchanged by rotation and reflection; flip axes freely to make the map readable, and decide flips from the data, not by hard-coding them.
4. **Forgetting `coord_equal()` / `asp = 1`.** Unequal axis scales distort distances on the plot.
5. **Comparing `isoMDS()` stress with stress values reported as proportions.** `isoMDS()` reports percent.
:::

## 8. Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q1. Classical MDS on a dissimilarity matrix returns some negative eigenvalues. What does that tell you?

The dissimilarities are **not Euclidean**: no configuration of points in any dimension reproduces them exactly. If the negative eigenvalues are small relative to the leading positive ones, a low-dimensional map can still be a good approximation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q2. Two analysts get mirror-image MDS maps from the same distances. Who is right?

Both. Reflections (and rotations) leave all distances unchanged, so both configurations fit equally well.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Q3. When would you prefer non-metric MDS to classical MDS?

When only the **rank order** of the dissimilarities is trustworthy (ratings, rankings, many similarity judgements), or when the relation between dissimilarity and distance is expected to be non-linear.
:::

## 9. Exercises

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 1 — MDS of Euclidean distances = PCA.** Compute the Euclidean distances between the 150 flowers of `iris` after standardising the four measurements (`dist(scale(iris[, 1:4]))`). Run `cmdscale(..., k = 2, eig = TRUE)` and compare the coordinates with the first two PCA scores of `prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)`. Are there negative eigenvalues?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
d_iris <- dist(scale(iris[, 1:4]))
mds_iris <- cmdscale(d_iris, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
pca_iris <- prcomp(iris[, 1:4], scale. = TRUE)
all.equal(abs(unname(mds_iris$points)), abs(unname(pca_iris$x[, 1:2])))
range(mds_iris$eig)      # smallest values are ~0 (rounding), not truly negative
```
The coordinates coincide up to sign: classical MDS of Euclidean distances is PCA. Apart from numerical rounding (tiny values around ±1e-13), there are no negative eigenvalues.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★]{.stars} **Exercise 2 — predict.** You multiply all entries of `eurodist` by 0.621 to convert kilometres into miles and rerun `cmdscale()`. What happens to (a) the shape of the map, (b) the eigenvalues, (c) the GOF?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) Same shape, just scaled by 0.621. (b) Eigenvalues are multiplied by 0.621² (they are in squared units). (c) GOF is unchanged — it is a ratio of eigenvalues.
```r
m_miles <- cmdscale(eurodist * 0.621, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
m_miles$eig[1] / mds_euro$eig[1]    # 0.621^2
m_miles$GOF
```
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 3 — debug.** This code is supposed to draw the map with north at the top, but on a colleague's computer Stockholm ends up at the bottom. Why, and how would you make it robust?

```r
pts <- cmdscale(eurodist)
pts[, 2] <- -pts[, 2]
plot(pts, type = "n", asp = 1); text(pts, labels(eurodist))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
The sign of each MDS axis is arbitrary and can differ between computers or R/BLAS versions; the code flips axis 2 *unconditionally*. Decide the flip from the data:
```r
pts <- cmdscale(eurodist)
if (pts["Stockholm", 2] < pts["Athens", 2]) pts[, 2] <- -pts[, 2]
if (pts["Lisbon", 1] > pts["Athens", 1]) pts[, 1] <- -pts[, 1]
plot(pts, type = "n", asp = 1); text(pts, labels(eurodist), cex = 0.7)
```
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★]{.stars} **Exercise 4 — a third dimension.** Run classical MDS of `eurodist` with `k = 3`. How much do GOF₁ and GOF₂ increase compared with `k = 2`? Is the third dimension worth keeping?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
cmdscale(eurodist, k = 2, eig = TRUE)$GOF
cmdscale(eurodist, k = 3, eig = TRUE)$GOF
```
The third eigenvalue is much smaller than the first two (about 1.5 million vs 19.5 and 11.9 million), so GOF increases only modestly (GOF₂ from about 0.87 to about 0.91, GOF₁ from about 0.75 to about 0.79). For a geographic map two dimensions are the natural choice; the extra dimension mostly absorbs distortions of the road network.
:::
:::

::: {.exercise}
[★★★]{.stars} **Exercise 5 — mixed data with Gower distance.** Penguins are described by numeric measurements *and* categorical variables (island, sex). The **Gower** dissimilarity handles both: numeric differences are divided by the variable's range, categorical variables contribute 0 (same) or 1 (different), and everything is averaged. (a) Compute the Gower dissimilarity with `cluster::daisy(..., metric = "gower")` on `island, sex, bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass` (complete cases). (b) Run classical MDS and colour the points by species. (c) Are there negative eigenvalues? (d) What do the two dimensions seem to capture?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```r
peng <- penguins |>
  select(species, island, sex, bill_len, bill_dep, flipper_len, body_mass) |>
  na.omit()

d_gower <- cluster::daisy(peng |> select(-species), metric = "gower")
mds_g <- cmdscale(d_gower, k = 2, eig = TRUE)
sum(mds_g$eig < 0)
mds_g$GOF

data.frame(mds_g$points, species = peng$species, sex = peng$sex) |>
  ggplot(aes(X1, X2, colour = species, shape = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  coord_equal()
```
There are many negative eigenvalues (Gower dissimilarity is not Euclidean) and GOF₁ is clearly smaller than GOF₂. In the map, one dimension separates **Gentoo** (different island and body shape) from Adelie and Chinstrap, which largely overlap; the other dimension separates **females from males** — the categorical variable `sex` creates a 0/1 jump that dominates a whole dimension. That is a property of the Gower distance worth remembering: categorical variables can weigh a lot.
:::
:::

## Summary

| Idea / function | What it does |
|---|---|
| `dist()`, `as.dist()` | build a dissimilarity object |
| `cmdscale(d, k, eig = TRUE)` | classical (metric) MDS: `points`, `eig`, `GOF` |
| negative `eig` | the dissimilarities are not Euclidean |
| `GOF` | $\sum_{i \le k}\lambda_i$ over $\sum|\lambda_i|$ and over $\sum \max(\lambda_i, 0)$ |
| Shepard diagram | original vs fitted distances |
| `MASS::isoMDS()` | non-metric MDS; stress in percent |
| `cluster::daisy(metric = "gower")` | dissimilarity for mixed numeric/categorical data |

- MDS turns a table of dissimilarities into a **map** whose distances approximate them.
- Classical MDS of Euclidean distances **is PCA**; non-Euclidean inputs give **negative eigenvalues**.
- Orientation and signs are arbitrary: **flip axes based on the data** to make the map readable.
- Judge the map with **GOF**, a **Shepard diagram** and, for non-metric MDS, **stress**.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon="false"}
## Further reading

- Borg, I. & Groenen, P., *Modern Multidimensional Scaling* (2nd ed.), Springer.
- R documentation: `?cmdscale`, `?MASS::isoMDS`, `?cluster::daisy`.
:::
